title: An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning
abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) define a distribution through a scalar energy, $p_\theta(x)\propto\exp(-E_\theta(x))$, and are usually presented as one model family among many. This tutorial has a broader goal: beyond introducing EBMs, it uses them as a single lens that connects the different aspects of machine learning. Any EBM is specified by three choices, the energy, which determines what the model represents; the inference procedure, which samples from or optimizes the energy; and the learning method, which fits the energy to data. We first develop these components, including sampling, variational inference, and learning by maximum likelihood, noise contrastive estimation, pseudolikelihood, score matching, and adversarial training, and show that the learning methods share one contrastive structure. We then show that discriminative models, generative models such as GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion and autoregressive models, representation learning methods such as contrastive learning, word2vec, BERT, denoising auto-encoders, and diffusion representations, reinforcement learning with EBM policies and world models, inverse reinforcement learning, and planning, as well as inference-time computation with verifiers, are all EBMs that differ in these three choices, mostly in how they handle the partition function and sampling. This view explains existing methods, organizes them into a common framework, and suggests new algorithms by replacing one component while keeping the others, with composition of energies as a principled way to combine learned models at inference time.
authors: ["Bo Dai", "Yilun Du"]

title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/
authors: ["Amani Kiruga", "Zhiyi Li", "Ruojin Cai", "Hansen Lillemark", "Xiaoshan Wu", "Ayush Tewari", "Yilun Du"]

title: Interpretable Weight-Space Programming Builds Transparent Transformers and Brain Encoding Models
abstract: Neural networks are powerful predictors, yet their opacity limits their usefulness in science, where the goal is explanation rather than mere prediction. In neuroscience, for example, deep encoding models accurately predict brain activity in response to natural stimuli, but struggle to reveal which stimulus features drive those predictions. Here we introduce interpretable weight-space programming (iWSP), a method in which an LLM agent iteratively builds interpretable models by explicitly programming their weights and features in code, without gradient-based training (backpropagation). Without backpropagation to tune parameters, the agent must draw on its prior knowledge and reason over previous trials to hypothesize, “hand-craft”, and refine human-interpretable computations mirroring the workflow of a human scientist. LLM audits confirm the interpretability of the hand-crafted models. We first validate iWSP by tasking it with constructing transformers for canonical benchmarks such as arithmetic and sentiment classification, finding that LLM agents can successfully craft compact, accurate networks directly. Next, we apply iWSP to build neural encoding models across vision, language, and audition. In the visual cortex, iWSP outpredicts existing interpretable baselines, uncovers distinct computations across early/higher visual areas, and generalizes to unseen data. In language fMRI, iWSP surfaces a confound in the data and in auditory ECoG, it systematically discovers interpretable acoustic features that predict neural activity. Together, these results establish iWSP as a general paradigm for aligning high predictive performance with human-interpretable scientific discovery.
authors: ["Yash Mehta", "Chandan Singh", "Weijia Xu", "Richard J. Antonello", "Adeen Flinker", "Nima Mesgarani", "Michael F. Bonner", "Nebojsa Jojic", "Jianfeng Gao"]

title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding
abstract: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.
authors: ["Ellis Brown", "Chris Hoang", "Shengyi Qian", "Shang-Wen Li", "Mike Lewis", "Marjan Ghazvininejad", "Luke Zettlemoyer", "Lucas Beyer", "Mengye Ren", "Jakob Verbeek", "Saining Xie", "Hu Xu"]

title: Weight-Space Reading
abstract: Can a language model predict what an edit to a network’s weights will do to its behavior, without running the network? We call this weight-space reading, the reading half of Weight-Space Programming, and test it with sandboxed reader agents that inspect the weights of Qwen3.8-27B (27B), Qwen3.5-9B (9B), and Muse-Glimmer-30B (Muse-30B) over three pre-registered rounds. Given only the weights and a Python sandbox, 27B predicts the behavioral effects of subtle, non-destructive edits to its own weights at 0.730 balanced accuracy, against 0.578 when given a text description of the same edits (+0.152, 95% CI [+0.056, +0.256]), and recovers two thirds of the real behavior changes against about a quarter, zero-shot and without a single forward pass. Three findings qualify this capability. We find no conclusive evidence of a self-reading advantage: the crossed self-reading contrast includes zero in every round, while a stronger external reader, 27B, outperforms Muse-30B on its own weights (0.615 vs. 0.468 balanced accuracy; 95% CI of the difference [+0.027, +0.258]). The readers we tested did not notice when an edit did nothing: none of 40 edits (34 standard edits and 6 no-op controls) changed Muse-30B’s behavior, yet readers given its weights predicted a change for 53–88% of them, Muse-30B itself for 85%. Benchmarks built from destructive edits measure damage detection: on such edits a model from another family predicts the effects of edits to 27B as well as 27B itself (0.594 vs. 0.593). We distill four rules for evaluating weight reading and release the evaluation harness.
authors: ["Şuayp Talha Kocabay"]

title: SLAM Dunk: A Recipe for Long-Horizon Egocentric SLAM in the Wild
abstract: Standard visual-inertial odometry (VIO) systems struggle to maintain accuracy with long trajectories in the wild, especially in egocentric settings, as evidenced by the gap between prior art and industry systems on the LaMAria benchmark. We find that a conventional offline bundle adjustment pipeline closes much of this gap, but plateaus at the level of strong public submissions, well below Aria’s SLAM. We hypothesize that the remaining gap occurs because standard VIO models omit two physical phenomena: camera calibration drift and gyroscope intrinsic calibration. We introduce SLAM Dunk, a pipeline for long-horizon ego-centric SLAM that models these sensor effects. SLAM Dunk becomes the first to outperform Aria’s SLAM on three out of the five LaMAria test categories. It also achieved first place on the UZH-FPV leaderboard at submission. Code is available at https://github.com/jacobvm04/slam-dunk.
authors: ["Jacob Van Meter", "Ayush Paul"]

title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $\pi_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $\pi_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.
authors: ["Jiaming Tang", "Zhuoyang Zhang", "Junxian Guo", "Fangzhou Zhao", "Yilong Zhao", "Zekai Li", "Xingyang Li", "Yuyang Zhao", "Song Bian", "Zhijian Liu", "Song Han"]

title: Weight-Space Programming Doesn’t Need Transformers
abstract: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800× fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17× faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.
authors: ["Hyunjong Ok", "Jaeho Lee"]

title: Latent Feedback Is a Compute and Data Amplifier
abstract: When high-quality data runs out, a common practice is to train on it for several epochs, but each repeat is worth less than the last. Latent feedback, which feeds each token's top-layer state into the next token's input, is another way to spend that compute, yet it has not been tested against a vanilla Transformer that spends the same compute on more epochs. We run this test across a ladder of model sizes, unique data and epochs, tuning both models at every size and amount of unique data. Latent feedback makes every FLOP and every token count for more except when unique data is scarce relative to model size, a regime that today's models are far from. We find that latent feedback serves as an amplifier: with unique data fixed, it reaches a Transformer's loss with less compute; with epochs fixed, it reaches that loss with less unique data. Furthermore, both savings grow with unique data per parameter and with repetition, and downstream tasks agree. To go beyond our grid, we fit one scaling law to both models, in which latent feedback enters as a Transformer with more parameters; it predicts that both savings keep growing with unique data and repetition. Fitted on models from 60M to 271M parameters, the law predicts the losses at a held-out 778M size to within 0.3% and the gap between the two models to within 0.05%. At most, latent feedback saves 48% of the compute and 47% of the unique data. When data, not compute, is the limit, latent feedback is the better use of a FLOP for a model of a given size.
authors: ["Benhao Huang", "Chaitanya Dwivedi", "Xuezhe Ma", "Alexander Moreno", "Hector Liu"]

title: ScaleVLA: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models to 552 Billion Parameters
abstract: Frontier Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robot control, suggesting that broad pretraining provides knowledge valuable for physical action. Yet most Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies still rely on much smaller VLM backbones, leaving this potential largely untapped. We ask whether frontier-scale representations can provide a stronger foundation for robot learning. We introduce ScaleVLA, which connects a 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone to a trainable action DiT, and systematically compare VLMs from 2B to 552B under a shared training setup. We evaluate three fundamental capabilities of robot foundation models. In sample efficiency, just 10 demonstrations outperform a 2B backbone trained with 50 (87.8% vs. 85.6%). In generalization, LIBERO-PRO success reaches 45.1%, compared with at most 31.3% for smaller backbones. In precise manipulation, real-world charger insertion improves from 4/10 to 9/10 successes, with gains concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment. Despite its scale, ScaleVLA achieves 216 ms median latency per action chunk. Our findings suggest that frontier VLMs can serve not only as reasoning agents, but also as powerful representational foundations for efficient and generalizable robot policies.
authors: ["Ruixi Yu", "Dairu Liu", "Xuchuan Chen", "Zekun Qi", "Zekai Li", "Zhuo Cao", "Luyang Niu", "Yingsheng Zhang", "Sikai Liang", "Ke Fan", "He Wang", "Li Yi"]

title: $π^4$: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion
abstract: $\pi^4$ is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild---a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence---it recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. It couples a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch, which predicts image-space correspondences that are lifted into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry. Across diverse benchmarks, $\pi^4$ achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation, alongside competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation. With a shared backbone, the full geometry-and-motion system contains approximately 0.5B parameters---less than half the size of most baselines. It produces joint reconstructions and tracks in one forward pass, including large-scale scenes with thousands of input images despite training with contexts of at most 64 views. We further present the data and training recipe underlying these capabilities, together with empirical studies of key design choices. Code and models are available at https://github.com/yyfz/Pi4.
authors: ["Yifan Wang", "Weiguang Zhao", "Ni Yang", "Haoyu Guo", "Junting Dong", "Weinan Zhang", "Chunhua Shen"]

title: A Society of AI Scientists
abstract: Artificial intelligence agents can now conduct end-to-end research, yet whether independent agents can collaborate, critique peer findings and build cumulative knowledge as a scientific community remains unclear. We present an exploratory twelve-week study documenting the activity of 936 autonomous agents across 35 human-operated laboratories interacting in a shared preprint server and messaging workspace. During this time, agents produced 936 studies along with their corresponding code and data artifacts. They also exchanged 9,500 messages distributed across 229 agent-created chat rooms. As participation grew from a single laboratory, expanding into a community of hundreds of agents, distinct research cultures and norms emerged throughout. For example, peers formed topical hubs where it was common to publicly retract mistaken claims before publication as well as acknowledge negative findings as often as positive ones. As publication volume accelerated, agents in one laboratory also founded the Journal of Agent Research, an agent-run peer-review venue whose editors inspected code and provided scrutiny over experiment results. Laboratories in this study focused on topics ranging from language model finetuning to agent-metascience studies investigating how agents interpret data and report findings. Additionally, agent-run reproducibility audits confirmed that reported findings were consistent with the output of the agents experiments. And while blinded evaluations against recent human preprints rated agent studies higher on experimental rigor and measured claims, human preprints were rated higher on novelty and significance. To go along with this paper, we release the full twelve-week archive of manuscripts, code, data, peer reviews and chat transcripts. Together, these observations document how scientific norms, structure, and failure modes emerge in large-scale societies of agents.

title: Counterfactual World Models: JEPAs That Reason About "What If"
abstract: World models operate in a world they cannot fully observe. When a hidden disturbance, such as a current pushing a boat, changes the outcome of an action, a counterfactual question follows: what would have happened under a different action, subject to the same disturbance? Its answer separates bad decisions from bad luck. We prove that world models trained on factual transitions cannot answer it on their own, whatever their data or capacity. For many physical systems, the observed outcome and a simple property of the dynamics suffice: natura non facit saltus, nature makes no leaps. When actions and disturbances act as separate forces, their interaction is second-order in time, so the counterfactual outcome is, to first order, the observed outcome plus the difference between the world model's predictions under the alternative and factual actions. This yields a counterfactual world model with no counterfactual data, extra parameters, or retraining. For transitions of duration $h$, we prove an $O(h^2)$ bound on the counterfactual error relative to the disturbance variance, establish a matching minimax lower bound from unpaired factual data, and characterize failures at discontinuities, coordinate folds, and disturbances that scale the command. We validate these predictions from pixels with JEPA world models on frozen DINOv2 and masked autoencoder (MAE) encoders. On four rendered simulators, our approach improves counterfactual $R^2$ from $38$--$46\%$ to $86$--$96\%$ with the same world models; on a fifth, an underwater vehicle, it reaches $90$--$94\%$ with sixteen times more factual data. Four further frozen encoders, DINOv3, SigLIP~2, CLIP and EVA-02, give $81$--$95\%$ on the same simulators. In hindsight planning, it finds the action that would have reached the goal in $35$--$69\%$ of events, against $14$--$23\%$ for an oracle planner that knows the simulator but not the outcome.
authors: ["Randall Balestriero", "Yann LeCun", "Kerda Varaku"]

title: The Content–Geometry Tradeoff in World Models: When JEPA Learns Latent Maps
abstract: A latent world model for planning needs two properties: latent distances that smoothly track progress toward a goal (geometry), and task-relevant factors that remain decodable from the latent representation (content). Common approaches prevent representation collapse with a stop-gradient (SG) target or a distributional regularizer, but we find that both often yield poor latent geometry. In this paper, we introduce sliced variance regularization (SVReg), which imposes a variance floor on latent projections along random directions. SVReg learns a smooth map of the agent’s state. Its latent trajectories are smooth, and its latent distances track progress in navigation and reaching. These geometric benefits, however, can come with a tradeoff in content. SVReg can discard slowly changing, hard-to-predict factors, such as the pose of a manipulated object, that SG variants tend to preserve. To address this tradeoff, we propose Slow SVReg, which favors slowly changing factors with a slowness term and a gated residual predictor. It keeps these factors and improves planning. This simple recipe has the highest planning success in the hard settings of five visual control tasks, and it learns latent maps from first-person mazes and city walks.
authors: ["Mengye Ren", "Ying Wang", "Christopher Hoang", "Yilun Kuang", "Yann LeCun"]

title: Language Model Harnesses Can Be Compositional Generalizers
abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are post-trained and deployed as agents inside a “harness”, but standard harness designs accumulate context that the neural network is forced to generalize to, making training for long-horizon tasks expensive and time-consuming. We study an alternative emerging path: training inherently neurosymbolic LM harnesses, which externalize and manage context programmatically to compose existing LM capabilities. We hypothesize that training around these harnesses can offer a better return on compute by enabling compositional generalization, as they can learn to decompose complex problems so that every observation their neural LM receives is locally in-distribution, even when the full task is novel. We find that harnesses like the Recursive Language Model (RLM) learn such decompositions readily under reinforcement learning post-training: (1) we demonstrate that training only on short tasks can generalize to tasks 2–64× longer while the base neural LM improves less, and (2) training on one domain transfers to novel domains that share latent structure. On messier, complex tasks, we find that we can target individual LLM calls within a harness by generating and training on easier, synthetically generated surrogate environments with fake tool / sub-calls, a technique we call surrogate harness training. From this finding, we train RLM-27B on synthetic data, and show it improves Qwen3.8-27B in the same RLM harness on a hard suite of long-context tasks like CTC-Bench and ExpertLongBench by 26.9% on average while using ∼2× fewer tokens at inference time. Finally, we show that harnesses can compose over these newly learned decompositions using recursive sub-harness calls.
authors: ["Alex L. Zhang", "Souradip Chakraborty", "Omar Khattab"]

title: Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts: Toward Continual Post-Training
abstract: RL post-training typically produces domain experts that must then be consolidated into one model, and as new experts keep arriving, this consolidation becomes a continual process. Weight merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) must re-consolidate the whole model whenever an expert is added, and can erode capabilities outside the target domains. We propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD), which keeps the pre-RL model frozen, distills each RL expert independently into a soft prompt, and composes experts by concatenating their prompts without joint training. A single soft prompt suffices to distill an RL expert, recovering at least 90% of the teacher’s gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings. Independently trained prompts compose well. In a multi-expert setting, the average rises with every expert added, and the full composition matches MOPD (67.83 vs. 67.79). The composition generalizes best across six held-out benchmarks. Input-space adaptation adds little serving overhead, keeping throughput within 1.5% of the unadapted backbone and reaching 2.40× that of rank-4 LoRA. These results point toward continual post-training on a fixed backbone. Code is available at https://github.com/UCSB-AI/CSPD.

title: A Claimed Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis
abstract: Levent Alpöge claims to have discovered, with Claude, a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and says the arguments have been formalized. The text describes a proposed method involving Fourier-analytic ideas, theta lifts, and an analogy with Stepanov’s argument over function fields. The author says the proof is long and intends to explain and simplify it.
authors: ["Levent Alpöge"]
cluster_name: AI-driven mathematical reasoning and formal theorem proving

title: Verifiable On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful approach for improving language-model reasoning, but its supervision is inherently sparse: a sequence-level verifier reward is propagated only through sampled trajectories and provides no direct signal for alternative actions. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a complementary form of supervision by providing dense teacher feedback over the full next-token distribution, but this signal is not grounded in verified task outcomes. Simply co-optimizing the two objectives does not couple these signals: verifier feedback remains sparse and does not inform the dense teacher supervision. We introduce Verifiable On-Policy Distillation (VOPD), which transfers sparse verifier feedback into dense, verifier-grounded supervision. Our key observation is that the implicit-reward view of OPD places teacher supervision and verifier feedback in a common reward space while retaining a reward signal available for every next-token action. Under this view, VOPD projects verifier preference onto the teacher's implicit-reward direction and Rao--Blackwellizes the resulting signal over the full vocabulary, propagating verifier-grounded supervision to actions that were never sampled. The resulting objective can also be interpreted as adaptively extrapolating the distillation target according to teacher--verifier agreement. Across two teacher--student configurations and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VOPD consistently improves both final performance and learning efficiency over vanilla OPD and other on-policy distillation baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/juntongshi48/VOPD.
authors: ["Juntong Shi", "Stefano Ermon", "Jure Leskovec", "Minkai Xu"]
